claims.text: Scarlet macaws reached Chaco through a long-distance Indigenous exchange network.
claims.explanation: The line is a macroregional connection, not a known road or identified supply settlement. Ancient DNA later suggested an undiscovered breeding community outside the species' natural range; individual birds need not have travelled directly from tropical Mesoamerica. 1150 is the sampled acquisition span, not a universal end to Indigenous trade.

sources.title: Obsidian and volcanic glass artifact evidence for long-distance voyaging to the Polynesian Outlier island of Tikopia
sources.authors: Mark D. McCoy, Caroline Cervera, Mara A. Mulrooney, Andrew McAlister and Patrick V. Kirch
sources.access: Publisher abstract read; detailed artifact table not accessed.

review.summary: Chemical analysis identifies Tongan volcanic glass reaching Tikopia from around 765 calibrated years before 1950, with stated dating uncertainty. A connection with Tongan political expansion is proposed, but transported material alone does not establish political control.
review.limitations: Map placement is a schematic anchor for Tikopia, southeastern Solomon Islands, not a verified site coordinate. No resident population estimate, fixed ethnic identity or exact voyage route is inferred. Access limits are recorded for each source.
review.discussion: Different evidence types address different questions; model results do not become direct observations of an arrival or language boundary.
review.provenance: Reviewed against primary material from three overlapping Pacific-origins exports and one Fiji export; canonical Hawaiʻi chronology/network records belong to the coordinated reviewer. Full author-supplied synthesis archive: docs/intake/index.html. Original synthesis is secondary provenance, not a substitute for the cited primary study.

location.precision: Regional reference at Niuatoputapu. The data do not name a specific source island or outcrop.
location.provenance: GeoNames public Niuatoputapu island reference, https://www.geonames.org/search.html?country=TO&q=&startRow=0. McCoy et al. discuss the broader northern Tongan source region.

destination.name: Tikopia, Solomon Islands
destination.precision: Island-scale reference. Individual excavation units are named in the evidence.
destination.provenance: GeoNames feature 2178465 (CC BY 4.0), rounded. https://www.geonames.org/2178465/ — Swift et al. 2021, Figure 1 identifies the Sinapupu area and excavation zones.

time.original: Published approximate import onset 765 cal BP (±54); independent modeled Tuakamali phase onset 1158–1212 cal CE (95% HPD).
time.method: The authors associate the three pieces with Tuakamali contexts at TK-1 and TK-35. The line uses the radiocarbon-based onset of that phase as an approximate anchor for the earliest possible exchange evidence.
time.interpretation: The window marks uncertainty around the emergence of Tongan-source imports. The precise arrival of each piece and the end of contact are unknown.

overlay.precision: The line connects generalized source and find references. It represents the direction of material movement.
overlay.provenance: Endpoints follow the locations above. The material connection is documented by Mark D. McCoy, Caroline Cervera, Mara A. Mulrooney, Andrew McAlister and Patrick V. Kirch.

claims.text: Three volcanic-glass pieces from the Tuakamali phase on Tikopia match Tongan reference material. The source study places them in excavated deposits and identifies northern Tonga as the likely source region.
claims.explanation: Available analyses cannot select a Tongan island or outcrop. The glass does not independently establish when particular people arrived or the kind of political relationship they had.

review.summary: Three volcanic-glass pieces from the Tuakamali phase on Tikopia match Tongan reference material. The source study places them in excavated deposits and identifies northern Tonga as the likely source region.
review.limitations: Available analyses cannot select a Tongan island or outcrop. The glass does not independently establish when particular people arrived or the kind of political relationship they had.
review.discussion: Most analyzed volcanic glass on Tikopia came from the Banks Islands. The rarer Tongan glass adds evidence of a different connection in deposits associated with changes in tools and ornament. McCoy and colleagues proposed a link to Tongan political expansion, which remains an interpretation.

updates.reason: Replace the single display year of 1185 with a schematic northern-Tonga-to-Tikopia source connection anchored to the original modeled transition range.
